newsitem.title: USA: Mobutu departure may open way for peace, U.S. says.
newsitem.headline: Mobutu departure may open way for peace, U.S. says.

text.p: The United States said on Friday the departure of President Mobutu Sese Seko from Kinshasa made possible a peaceful end to the Zaire conflict.
"We believe that his departure now opens the way for a peaceful resolution of the military conflict," Secretary of State Madeleine Albright told reporters.
She and President Bill Clinton said Washington's priority was to see a peaceful transition to a democratic government in the central African state.
Clinton pledged to "do what we can to support Africa in taking one of the the largest and most important nations in Africa and promoting a democratic transition. That is what I think is important."

As rebel forces advanced towards Kinshasa, Mobutu left the capital on Friday for his native village in northern Zaire and an official statement said he would no longer take any part in the government of the country.
One official said the U.S. ambassador in Kinshasa was told on Thursday that Mobutu had been informed that his forces could not defend the capital against rebel forces.

"Our ambassador, Dan Simpson, was called last night by one of Mobutu's colleagues, who said that Mobutu's military advisers met with him yesterday and said they could not defend the capital, and they couldn't defend him in the capital. And they advised him to leave...," the official said. He declined to be identified.
The Clinton administration has been saying for weeks that the Mobutu era is over, making clear it has withdrawn support for the autocratic leader.

Washington and other western states backed Mobutu for decades as he upheld their interests in African struggles that were often proxy battles between the major western and communist powers in the Cold War.

"We are at this stage working with all the parties so that we can avoid bloodshed and also to do what can be done in terms of contributing to a process that would be peaceful and have an inclusive transition that would result in free and fair elections," Albright said.

Clinton called for worldwide support for the efforts of South African leader Nelson Mandela to end the violence. He told reporters at the White House that Mandela had done "a superb job" in trying to end the fighting.

Mandela has consulted regularly with African leaders and the British, U.S. and French governments in his efforts to avert a military showdown in Kinshasa between Mobutu's government forces and Laurent Kabila's rebel army.
But neither he nor Clinton's envoy, U.N. Ambassador Bill Richardson, have succeeded in persuading Mobuto and Kabila to accept a negotiated settlement and stop the fighting.
State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Richardson was trying to arrange a meeting with Kabila on Friday.

A military force was still standing by in the region in case it was needed to help the 25 personnel at the U.S. embassy and 310 private Americans still in the country, Burns said. The official advice to them was to get out of the country if they safely could.

He said if the United States saw in the transition "a good faith effort to lead Zaire out of its current troubles towards a democratic future," it would be prepared to offer political and financial support to a "reform government".

But Burns said: "We are at a time of testing for Mr Kabila. He does not have a track record as a government leader. He has held a variety of political and ideological positions throughout his long career in opposition.
"And we hope that he will be a responsible leader who believes in what the Zairean people deserve. And that is economic reform and reconstruction and political freedom."
